templates.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues

canonical.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ - 3 & 4\end{array} \right]}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $4.$*
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=t, \qquad
\lambda_2=4t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(4t) &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
3t\alpha_1 = e^{4t} - e^{t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{3t}\bigl(e^{4t}-e^{t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $4$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
3\alpha_0 = 4e^{t} - e^{4t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{3}\bigl(4e^{t}-e^{4t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}+4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={e}^{t} \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{4t} \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((4{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{t})+(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t})) \\  & ={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
e^{At} = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ {e}^{t} - {e}^{4 t} & {e}^{4 t}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

nearby_inspected.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 7{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ r(t) &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-5t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the second equation by $4$ and adding to the first one, we get

$$
5{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6\left(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-6{e}^{-4t}+6{e}^{t}))+({e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{-4t}-2{e}^{t}) \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2\left(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{e}^{-4t}-2{e}^{t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}7{e}^{-4t}-2{e}^{t} & -7{e}^{-4t}+7{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}-2{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{-4t}+7{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -6 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=0,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ r(0) &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=1.
$$

- Substituting ${\alpha }_{0}=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}+1={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-6\left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1)\right)t+1 \\  & =\frac{6}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{-3+3{e}^{-4t}+2}{2} \\  & =\frac{-1+3{e}^{-4t}}{2} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1)\right)t \\  & =-\frac{2}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1+3{e}^{-4t} & -3+3{e}^{-4t} \\ 1-{e}^{-4t} & 3-{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}7 & 4 \\ - 5 & - 1\end{array} \right]}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $3 \pm 2\textrm{i}.$*
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1= (3+2\textrm{i}) t, \qquad
\lambda_2= (3-2\textrm{i}) t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((3+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(3+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(3+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)), \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
e^{At} = e^{3t}
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos   ( 2 t ) + 2 \sin   ( 2 t ) & 2 \sin   ( 2 t ) \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{5}{2}} \sin   ( 2 t ) & \cos   ( 2 t ) - 2 \sin   ( 2 t )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

nearby_inspected.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1\pm 4\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$ |  | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |
nearby_inspected.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 8{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & -3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(1+4\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(1-4\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((1+4\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(1+4\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(1+4\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ ({\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+4{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+{e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & =-4\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

nearby_inspected.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1\pm 2\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
nearby_inspected.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(-1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(-1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((-1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(-1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(-1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}8 & - 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{array} \right]}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $6,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
\lambda_1 = 6t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(6t) &={e}^{6t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(6t) &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{6t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
\alpha_1 = e^{6t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
6t e^{6t} + \alpha_0 = e^{6t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = e^{6t}(1-6t).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{6t}t+{e}^{6t}(1-6t) \\  & ={e}^{6t}(1+2t), \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{6t}t \\  & ={e}^{6t}(-2t), \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{6t}t \\  & ={e}^{6t}(2t), \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4{e}^{6t}t+{e}^{6t}(1-6t) \\  & ={e}^{6t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
e^{At} = 
e^{6t} 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 + 2 t & - 2 t \\ 2 t & 1 - 2 t\end{array} \right]}.
$$

nearby_inspected.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-t$ | $1-t$ |  |  |
nearby_inspected.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+t), \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1+t & t \\ -t & 1-t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

nearby_inspected.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |
nearby_inspected.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

backbone: Write e^(At)=alpha1 At+alpha0 I and expand all entries.
Interpolate r(lambda)=alpha1 lambda+alpha0 at eigenvalues of At; for a repeated eigenvalue include derivative interpolation.
Solve coefficients; complex conjugates use real/imaginary parts.
Substitute into required entries and extract supplied outer factor, then present whole matrix.
